title: Delivery and handoff
summary: How to hand over a client app so that someone else can run it, understand it and change it: a clean repo, short docs, safe access and a trained client.
youWillLearn: The four parts of a good handoff: repo, docs, access and training
The "stranger test" a clean repo must pass
How to hand over secrets without leaving copies in email or chat
How acceptance testing and a sign-off close the project

glossary.handoff: The package and moment where you transfer a finished project so others can run, understand and change it without you.
glossary.bus factor: How many people would have to disappear before nobody understands the project. One is fragile.
glossary.README: The front-page document of a repo: what the project is and how to run it.
glossary.migration: A file in the repo that records one change to the database structure, so every copy of the database can be rebuilt the same way.
glossary.password manager: An app that stores secrets encrypted and lets you share them with specific people, without pasting them into chat or email.
glossary.rotate: To replace a key or password with a new one and switch the old one off, so earlier copies stop working.
glossary.runbook: A short page of steps for a known situation: if this happens, check this, then do that.
glossary.UAT: User acceptance testing: the client checks the finished app against the agreed acceptance criteria.
glossary.sign-off: The client's written confirmation that the delivered work meets the agreed criteria.

steps.title: Sam's booking app is live
body: Sam owns a small hair salon. You built her booking app, and it is live: clients book online and get a text reminder before each visit.
Sam owns all the accounts it runs on. The project is nearly over, and soon you will step back. This lesson is about handing the app over well.

scene.caption: You built and run the booking app. Sam uses it every day.

steps.title: Launched, but it lives in your head
body: Only you know how to deploy the app (put a new version live), where the reminder timer runs, and why a test booking sits in the database.
That is a bus factor of one. If you get sick, or Sam hires a new developer, they must dig through your code to guess how it works. That reflects on you.
changes: + New Developer: someone Sam may hire later
~ You: the only one who knows how it works
~ Bus factor 1, and that is a risk

scene.caption: The app works, but the knowledge to run it sits with one person.

steps.title: A handoff is a package, not a call
body: A good handoff has four parts: a clean repo (the stored code), docs, access and training. Each answers a question someone will ask.
Can someone else run it? Do they know how it works? Can they get in? Can Sam do daily tasks without calling you? Plan these from week one, not on the last day.

callout.text: Selling a house. You hand over the keys, the manuals for the boiler, the name of the plumber and a note on which switch does what. Not just the address.

changes: − You and Booking App: we open the handoff package
+ Clean Repo, Docs, Access, Training: the four parts
~ New Developer gets repo and docs; Sam gets the rest

scene.caption: Four parts, two receivers: the new developer runs the app, Sam operates it.

steps.title: A clean repo passes the stranger test
body: The test: a stranger copies the repo, follows the README (its front-page guide), and has the app running on their laptop within an hour.
That needs a .env.example listing the keys, every database change saved as a migration, a seed file with fake data, and no dead experiments or stray test keys.

code.code:
git clone git@github.com:sams-salon/booking.git
cd booking
cp .env.example .env.local   # fill in dev keys
npm install
npx supabase start           # local database (needs Docker)
npx supabase db reset        # runs migrations, then seed
npm run dev
code.caption: Copy the code, add dev keys, install the packages, start a local database with fake data, run the app. If any step fails on a fresh laptop, the repo is not ready.

changes: ~ Clean Repo → New Developer: passes the stranger test
~ Handoff ready 0 of 4 → 1 of 4
~ Docs, Access, Training and Sam fade back

scene.caption: First part: a repo a stranger can run without asking you anything.

steps.title: Docs that answer real questions
body: Skip the essay. Write short answers to the questions people will ask: how do I deploy, what runs on a schedule, which services cost money, what are the known limits?
A one-page architecture sketch helps most. This is your strength as a designer: one clear diagram of the parts beats ten pages of prose.

code.code:
# Salon Booking
## Run locally       7 commands, see above
## Architecture      one diagram + 5 sentences
## Env vars          what each is, which account owns it
## Deploys           push to main = live site
## Scheduled jobs    reminders, every hour
## Running costs     hosting, database, SMS, AI
## Known limits      one location, English only

changes: ~ Docs: short answers and one diagram
~ Handoff ready 1 → 2 of 4
~ Bus factor 1 → 2: someone else can run and understand it

scene.caption: Second part: short docs, built around the questions people really ask.

steps.title: Hand over access, not passwords in chat
body: Sam already owns the accounts. What remains: secrets you created, and recovery codes for two-factor login. Share them through a password manager, never email or chat, which keep copies forever.
Cut your own access to what support needs. If you step away fully, remove yourself and have every key you saw rotated.

callout.text: Make sure at least two people on Sam's side can log in to every account, each with two-factor login. One owner with one phone is a single point of failure.

changes: ~ Access: secrets via a password manager, two admins for Sam
~ Handoff ready 2 → 3 of 4
~ New Developer fades back, Sam comes forward

scene.caption: Third part: secrets go through a password manager, and Sam has two admins.

steps.title: Train Sam on the daily jobs
body: Sam does not need to know the code. She needs to block a stylist's day off, cancel a booking, and know what to do when a client says "I never got a reminder".
Record a short screen video per task, and write a runbook: a page of "if this happens, do that" steps, including when to call you.

code.code:
1. Admin → Bookings: find the booking
2. Check "reminder sent at". Empty? Note the time.
3. SMS provider dashboard → message log
4. Still unclear? Email help@studio.example
   with the booking id. Reply within 1 business day.
code.caption: Written for Sam, in her words. No code, no jargon.

changes: ~ Training: short videos and a runbook for Sam
~ Handoff ready 3 → 4 of 4

scene.caption: Fourth part: Sam can run the salon's daily tasks on her own.

steps.title: Acceptance: Sam signs it off
body: Before the last invoice comes UAT, user acceptance testing: Sam checks each acceptance criterion from discovery on the live app, on real phones.
Each check passes or becomes a bug ticket, a written to-do for the fix. When all pass, she gives a written sign-off. That triggers the final payment and starts the warranty period from your contract.
changes: − Clean Repo, Docs, Access, Training, New Developer
+ Book Online, No Double-Book, Reminder Text: criteria
+ Sign-off: Sam's written OK, which releases the last payment

scene.caption: Sam tests every criterion. One fails and becomes a ticket; sign-off waits for it.

steps.title: Clean up what Claude Code left behind
body: AI-assisted repos collect leftovers: a forgotten test page, debug logs that print client phone numbers, commented-out code, TODO notes nobody owns.
Each costs the next developer time, and logs with personal data are a privacy problem. Do a cleanup pass before handoff, like tidying a Figma file before developers open it.

code.caption: Find debug prints, TODO notes, old branches (side copies of the code) and database changes missing from migrations.
code.code:
git grep -n "console.log"     # stray debug logs
git grep -nE "TODO|FIXME"     # unowned work
git branch -r                  # old branches
npx supabase db diff           # schema changes not in migrations

callout.text: Ask Claude Code for a handoff audit: unused files and pages, TODOs, logs that print personal data, env vars missing from .env.example. Review its list before fixing. Update CLAUDE.md, the notes file Claude Code reads first: it is the next developer's map.

changes: − Book Online, No Double-Book, Reminder Text, Sam, Sign-off
+ Code Repo: Sam's code, before your cleanup pass
+ Debug Logs, TODOs, Test Page: leftovers in it
+ Claude Code: runs a handoff audit

scene.caption: Leftovers point into the repo. A Claude Code audit finds them; you decide what goes.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: A handoff is a package: a repo a stranger can run, short docs with one diagram, access through a password manager with your keys rotated, and a runbook so Sam can operate without you.
Clean up AI leftovers first. Close with UAT against the original criteria and a written sign-off.
changes: − Debug Logs, TODOs, Test Page: cleaned up
~ Code Repo: ready to hand over
~ Claude Code: audit done

scene.caption: The leftovers are gone. The repo is ready for the next person.

quiz.question: Which is the best test that the repo is ready to hand over?

options.text: It deploys to the hosting without errors.
options.why: A working deploy says nothing about whether someone else can run, understand or change it.

options.text: A developer who has never seen it can run it locally from the README alone.
options.why: That is the stranger test. It proves the setup steps, env vars, migrations and seed data are all in the repo.

options.text: Claude Code says the code quality is good.
options.why: Useful as a check, but it does not prove someone can get the project running without your help.

quiz.question: Sam's new developer needs the SMS provider's API key for local development. What do you do?

options.text: Send it by email, then ask them to delete the email.
options.why: Email keeps copies on several servers and devices. Asking someone to delete it does not remove those.

options.text: Paste it into the README so it is easy to find.
options.why: The README is in the repo. Anyone with repo access, now or later, would have the key.

options.text: Share it through a password manager, or have Sam create a dev key for them.
options.why: A password manager shares it without leaving copies in chat or email. A separate dev key per developer is even better: it can be switched off on its own.

quiz.question: Claude Code's handoff audit lists 40 console.log calls (debug prints), two of which print a client's name and phone number. What matters most?

options.text: Remove the ones that print personal data first.
options.why: Logs are stored and often visible to more people than the database. Personal data in them is a privacy problem, not just mess.

options.text: Leave them all in; logs help with debugging.
options.why: Purposeful, structured logs help. Leftover debug prints, especially with personal data, do not.
Some logs may be intended, for example usage logging for AI costs. Review the list; do not delete blindly.

takeaways: A handoff has four parts: clean repo, docs, access, training. Plan them from week one.
A clean repo passes the stranger test: clone, follow the README, run it within an hour.
Share secrets through a password manager and reduce your own access. When you step away, get every key you saw rotated.
Give Sam a runbook and short videos for daily tasks, written in her words.
Close with UAT against the discovery criteria and a written sign-off.
